title: Vāmadevāya namaḥ: the second of the five ‘brahma’ mantras
theme: Eleven names of Śiva as Vāmadeva, each with namaḥ: the northern face, by the commentators’ account.

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «वामं सुन्दरं च तद्देवं दीप्यमानं चेति वामदेवं तस्मै» — lovely and shining
The anonymous commentator: «सर्वजगदुत्पत्तेः पूर्वभावित्वाज्ज्येष्ठाय» — because he exists before the world arises
The anonymous commentator: «प्रशस्ततमत्वाच्छ्रेष्ठाय» — the most praiseworthy
The anonymous commentator: «प्रलये रोदनहेतुत्वाद्रुद्राय» — the cause of weeping at the dissolution
The anonymous commentator: «सर्वप्राण्यायुःक्षयहेतुत्वात्कालाय» — the cause of the waning of every creature’s life

words.meaning: to the one who makes the manifold
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «कं सुखं लाति स्वी करोतीति कलं विविधं जगत्क्रियते येनेति विकरणं»

words.meaning: to the one who scatters strength
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «रक्षसां बलं विकीर्यते हिंस्यते येन तद्बलविकरणं तस्मै» — by whom the strength of demons is scattered

words.meaning: to the tamer of all beings
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «सर्वाणि भूतानि दमयति शिक्षयतीति सर्वभूतदमनं तस्मै» — who tames, disciplines all beings

words.meaning: to the one who uplifts the mind
words.context: Bhāskara: «मनोन्मनः मन्ता जीवः मनस् तस्योन्मानयिता उद्बोधकश् चैतन्योद्दीपकः»

sandhi.type: visarga after a before a voiced consonant
sandhi.rule: namaḥ + jyeṣṭhāya → namo jyeṣṭhāya: -aḥ becomes -o before a voiced sound; so namo before rudrāya, balavikaraṇāya, balāya, balapramathanāya, manonmanāya.
namaḥ stays before śreṣṭhāya (a visarga before a sibilant may stay); likewise before k (kālāya, kalavikaraṇāya).
namaḥ + sarva- → namas sarva-: the recitation writes the visarga as the sibilant, doubled (P. 8.3.36 (वा शरि)).

samasa.meaning: maker of the manifold of what is formed
the one who raises up the mind

morphology.note: Bhāskara takes vikaraṇa as an agent noun in -ana (‘the one who makes various’), citing P. 3.3.113 (कृत्यल्युटो बहुलम्), or as a bahuvrīhi; the anonymous commentator splits kala (‘what takes happiness’) and vikaraṇa.
Each name in the dative is followed by namaḥ: the regular formula of homage, ‘homage [be] to …’, with no verb.

translation.literal: To Vāmadeva homage; to the eldest homage; to the best homage; to Rudra homage; to Time homage; to the maker of the manifold homage; to the scatterer of strength homage; to Strength homage; to the crusher of strength homage; to the tamer of all beings homage; to the uplifter of the mind homage.
translation.readable: Homage to Vāmadeva, to the eldest, to the best, to Rudra, to Time; to the one who makes the manifold world, who scatters and who crushes strength, to Strength itself; to the tamer of all beings, and to the one who lifts up the mind.

syntax: A litany: eleven datives, each followed by namaḥ (‘homage [be] to …’). There is no verb; each pair is a complete sentence.

ambiguities.note: For the anonymous commentator all eleven are names of the one god of the northern face. Bhāskara reads them as the god with his powers, the first three standing for the powers of will, knowledge and action: «तत्रेच्छाज्ञानक्रियाशक्तिक्षोभका आद्यास्त्रयः».

The commentators explain the word differently: the anonymous commentator through kala, ‘what takes happiness’, and vikaraṇa, ‘that by which the various is made’; Bhāskara through kala as a stage of unmanifest change.

metre.name: prose
metre.note: A yajus: a list of names with namaḥ, not in metre.

beginner: This is the second of the five ‘brahma’ mantras that address five faces of Śiva. It is simply a list: eleven names, each followed by namaḥ, ‘homage’. The first name, Vāmadeva, means ‘the lovely god’; the old commentators identify him with the northern face. The other names describe what this god does: he is the eldest, because he existed before the world; the best; Rudra, who makes beings weep at the end of an age; Time, which wears away every life; the one who makes the world various; the one who breaks the strength of what is hostile; the tamer of all beings; and the one who lifts up the mind. Saying a list of names with ‘homage’ after each is a common Vedic form of praise. It needs no story; each name is a reason for the bow.
analogy: Like a roll call of a person’s titles before an audience, each one met with a bow.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It offers homage to Vāmadeva under eleven names: the eldest, the best, Rudra, Time, the maker of the manifold, the scatterer of strength, Strength, the crusher of strength, the tamer of all beings and the uplifter of the mind.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: the mantra that describes the northern face, «उत्तरवक्त्रप्रतिपादकमन्त्रमाह». He gives a reason for each name; Rudra, for example, «प्रलये रोदनहेतुत्वाद्रुद्राय», and Time, «सर्वप्राण्यायुःक्षयहेतुत्वात्कालाय».

commentary.q: How does Bhāskara read the list?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Bhāskara: these are not bodies of knowledge but the god with his powers, each called by its name: «वामदेवादयो न विद्याशरीराश् चितिशक्तेस् तत्तन्नाम्नीभिः शक्तिभिः सहिताः». The whole group is named after Vāmadeva because he comes first: «वामदेवप्राधान्याच्च न्यासादौ तेन समुदायस्याख्यानम्». The last name he explains as the one who wakes the conscious self: «मनोन्मनः मन्ता जीवः मनस् तस्योन्मानयिता उद्बोधकश् चैतन्योद्दीपकः».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: The Tirupati e-text reads balapramathāya for balapramathanāya (listed for review). Sāyaṇa’s own text, printed with his commentary, has no balāya namaḥ; his comment on this anuvāka is missing from the copy used, so only his text can be compared.

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this text is in the edition’s sources (Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not available here). The anonymous commentator explains each name of the one god of the northern face; Bhāskara reads the names as the god together with his powers. Neither draws a doctrine of the self from the list.

contemporary.text: A list of names, each followed by a bow, is a way of seeing one thing from many sides before acknowledging it. Naming what someone does, one act at a time, can be a more honest form of respect than a single general word. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: If you listed eleven names for someone you respect, what would they be?
reflect.deeper: The list moves from ‘the lovely god’ to Time and the tamer of beings, and ends with the uplifter of the mind. Why might it end there?
reflect.practice: Write down three things a person in your life does, and thank them for one.

references.text: Sāyaṇa’s file for his anuvāka 44 is a lacuna in the copy used (‘…’); his text of the mantra is printed with it.

flags.note: Tirupati: balapramathāya for balapramathanāya; the base and the Ānandāśrama text agree on the base reading.
No Sāyaṇa comment on this anuvāka is available (the file is a lacuna).
